title: The Ben & Jerry's story
voice: Every title, desc, comment or intro here is read by a player and is written as Envie speaking. See CLAUDE.md and _DESIGNS/envie-voice-and-text-rewrite-guide.md: plain short sentences, no em-dashes, European spelling, no emoji, facts and sources untouched. The optional 'envie' line on a slide is his own aside, one short sentence.

slides.text: It started in a converted petrol station in Vermont, sold out of vans just like this one.
slides.footer: It became one of the most values-driven brands on Earth.

slides.text: Before I go on, I should explain myself. I love ice cream. And Ireland does it properly, Teddy's up in Dún Laoghaire since 1950, Murphy's down in Dingle with milk from Kerry cows. So why am I banging on about an American brand?
slides.footer: Because of what its two founders did with the shop once they had one. That is the bit that stopped me.
slides.envie: I know. Stay with me a second.

slides.text: In 1978, childhood friends Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield opened an ice cream shop with a $12,000 investment, nearly half of it borrowed. A decade later, President Reagan named them US Small Business Persons of the Year.
slides.footer: But the real story isn't the ice cream. It's what they did with the platform it gave them.
slides.envie: Nearly half of it borrowed. Brave.

slides.text: Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield never stopped showing up in person for causes they believed in, long before 'purpose-driven business' was a marketing category.

When Pillsbury, the owner of rival Häagen-Dazs, pressured shared distributors to drop Ben & Jerry's, the pair didn't sue quietly. They flew banners over Boston stadiums and printed an 800-number on their tubs: 'What's the Doughboy Afraid Of?'
It set the template for the next four decades: turn customer goodwill into pressure, and use the brand itself as an activism tool, for refugee support, LGBTQ+ rights and climate justice.
slides.bold: the brand itself as an activism tool

slides.text: It backed LGBTQ+ rights in its flavours as much as its statements, an early corporate supporter of same-sex marriage years before it was safe to be.
slides.bold: years before it was safe to be

slides.title: Most brands market their values. Ben & Jerry's spent decades acting on them.
bad: Adopts a cause when it's convenient
Drops it when it gets costly
good: Criticised the Iraq War and backed Occupy Wall Street, all while under corporate ownership
Called to 'dismantle white supremacy' after George Floyd's murder
Built loyalty on shared values, not ad spend

slides.caption: In 2000, Unilever bought Ben & Jerry's for $326 million, on one condition: an independent board with legal authority over the brand's social mission, in perpetuity.
slides.note: Business schools cited the structure for years as a model for preserving purpose after acquisition.

slides.text: But the brand's clearest reputation is for taking a stand on someone else's issue: war, politics, human rights. Its own core product tells a harder story.
slides.footer: Dairy farming is one of the largest sources of methane on the planet.
slides.envie: Loud about far away, quiet about close to home. I've seen that before.

slides.callout: "It's a good question. I don't know."
slides.text: Asked whether Ben & Jerry's should tell customers plainly that milk and cream carry a real climate cost, co-founder Ben Cohen gave a disarmingly honest answer.
bullets: Not greenwashing: nothing here is misrepresented
But it's a real gap: a brand loud about Gaza or voting rights, quieter about its own best-selling product's emissions

slides.text: The ice cream is still rich and indulgent.
slides.footer: But like nearly all dairy, it carries a real climate cost worth talking about.

slides.caption: For nearly two decades, Ben & Jerry's 'Caring Dairy' programme has worked with farms in Vermont, the Netherlands, Germany and the UK on climate-smart practices, and it's since launched a full oat-based, non-dairy range.
slides.footer: A real step. Not yet the plain admission that the flagship product's cost is worth facing head-on.

slides.text: The relationship with Unilever broke down over Israel and Palestine.
bullets: 2021: the independent board voted to stop selling ice cream in the occupied West Bank, so Unilever sold the local trademark instead
2025: the ice cream business was spun off into a new company, Magnum
Jerry Greenfield resigned from the board in 2025, his first step away in nearly 50 years, writing that a company that can't stand up for what it believes 'isn't worth being a company at all'
slides.footer: The 'Free Ben & Jerry's' campaign, Cohen's push to buy the brand back, is still ongoing.

slides.text: The real test of authenticity isn't the causes a brand is loud about. It's the ones closer to home.
slides.footer: Magnum's growth rate, even as Ben & Jerry's keeps picking fights.
